hints: Count what you start and end with. You start with one double-stranded DNA molecule, so do you end with two separate single strands or two complete double-stranded molecules?
Think about building blocks. A single base is just one part (A, T, C or G), while a nucleotide is the full unit with deoxyribose sugar plus phosphate plus base that actually links to form a strand.
walkthrough:
**What does replication make?**

Think of replication like copying a zip. You start with one complete DNA molecule, which is two strands twisted together.

After copying, you have two complete identical DNA molecules, not just two loose strands. Each new molecule is double-stranded.

**What is each DNA strand built from?**

This is the key vocabulary check. A base on its own cannot form the backbone of DNA.

Each strand is a polynucleotide, meaning a long sequence of nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds. The bases pair across the middle (A with T, C with G), but the strands themselves are made of paired nucleotides.

**Put it together**

We need two (not one) plus molecules (not strands) plus nucleotides (not bases).

Only option B gives all three parts correctly: two molecules of DNA each made of a sequence of paired nucleotides.

options.A: Right number (two molecules) but wrong building block. DNA is not made of bases alone, it is made of nucleotides.
options.B: Exactly right. Replication of one double-stranded molecule produces two double-stranded molecules, and each strand is a sequence of nucleotides with complementary base pairing.
options.C: Wrong on both parts. The products are two whole molecules, not two single strands, and they are made of nucleotides, not bases alone.
options.D: Right building block (nucleotides) but wrong product. Two single strands alone would be only half a molecule each, replication makes two complete molecules.
